questions.q: What does the author say matters more than how much money you have?
a: What you actually do with it
How early you started earning
Which bank holds your savings
How much you know about taxes
questions.why: Lesson 1 argues that small sums still count, because your choices matter more than the balance.

questions.q: How did the couple earning under $50,000 manage to save and invest?
a: They lived on 65 percent of their income
They moved in with family for a year
They took second jobs at weekends
They invested all their savings at once
questions.why: Lesson 1 cites their example from Playing With FIRE, saving roughly $18,000 a year.

questions.q: What does the author say about avoiding risk?
a: Avoiding it also means avoiding wealth
It is the safest route to steady returns
It only makes sense once you are rich
It guarantees your money keeps its value
questions.why: Lesson 2 points out that money left untouched is guaranteed to stay put rather than grow.

questions.q: How should you handle the risk of an investment?
a: Keep each bet small enough to tolerate
Put everything in and wait for the result
Sell as soon as the price drops
Follow whoever sounds most confident
questions.why: Lesson 2 recommends making risks endurable, financially and emotionally, then waiting.

questions.q: Why does the author suggest exploring new asset classes?
a: The earlier you invest, the higher the potential returns
They are guaranteed by the government
They require no research or judgement
They always beat the stock market
questions.why: Lesson 3 ends by noting that early investors in brand new categories tend to do best.
